item.text: {"text":"The original [BERT4Rec paper](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.06690) mixes random masking with last-item-only training samples to improve alignment with appended-mask inference. Its one-mask ablation reduces supervision per sequence and still outperforms SASRec, but does not establish a terminal-versus-interior comparison jointly matched for optimizer updates, supervised-token counts, available context, and compute. Training duration is a major confound: the [replicability study](https://arxiv.org/html/2207.07483) needed up to 30× the default training duration to reproduce original results. A clean BERT4Rec experiment should therefore report separate comparisons at equal updates, equal supervised targets, and equal GPU time; keep architecture, loss, optimizer, user sampling, and context-length distributions fixed. These are proposed controls, not a protocol demonstrated by those papers.\n\n[Recency-based Sampling of Sequences](https://arxiv.org/html/2207.02643) controls wall-clock training at one hour, uses common sequence-length and optimizer settings for its experimental architectures, and varies target recency. Intermediate recency weighting improves accuracy over terminal-only continuation and uniform target selection in its experiments. However, RSS removes sampled targets and predicts a target set; it is not historical-prefix terminal masking, nor a direct BERT4Rec masking ablation. For prefix sampling, uniformly selecting historical endpoints broadens supervision beyond each user’s latest interaction and changes prefix lengths; weighting endpoints toward recent interactions increases recency emphasis. Whether either improves next-item accuracy remains dataset-dependent. To isolate inference alignment, compare terminal and interior masking while independently controlling endpoint sampling, visible-context length, and supervised targets per update; otherwise gains can reflect historical coverage, supervision volume, or compute."}
